title: Divide and Conquer
tagline: Split the problem in half, solve each half recursively, combine the results — and watch O(n²) brute-force collapse to O(n log n).

sections.content:
There is a moment in every programmer's education when a problem that seems hopelessly expensive suddenly collapses. You are trying to sort a million numbers, and the naive approach — compare every pair — costs a trillion operations. Then someone says: what if you split the array in half, sort each half, and merge the two sorted halves back together? The halves can be split again. And again. Down to single elements that need no sorting at all. This is **divide and conquer**, and it is one of the most powerful ideas in all of computer science.

Divide and conquer is a **recursive algorithm design paradigm** structured around three mandatory phases. **Divide**: decompose the problem into a set of smaller subproblems of the same type — usually two subproblems of half the original size. **Conquer**: solve each subproblem recursively. If a subproblem is small enough to solve directly (the base case), solve it without recursing. **Combine**: merge or assemble the subproblem solutions into a solution for the original problem. The correctness of the whole algorithm follows by induction: if the recursive calls produce correct solutions for smaller instances, and the combine step is correct, then the overall algorithm is correct.

The computational payoff comes from the logarithmic recursion depth. Halving a problem of size n at every level produces at most log₂ n levels before reaching the base case. If each level's total work is O(n) — as in merge sort's linear merge — then total work is O(n log n). That is a vast improvement over O(n²) brute force. Divide and conquer is responsible for merge sort, quicksort, binary search, quickselect, Strassen's matrix multiplication, fast Fourier transform, closest-pair-of-points, and dozens of other foundational algorithms.

Understanding divide and conquer means understanding three things: how to write the recursive structure, how to prove correctness via induction, and how to analyse complexity via recurrence relations and the master theorem. This chapter covers all three in depth, with worked examples and a tour of the most important algorithms in the family.

sections.title: Counting a City's Votes, District by District
sections.content:
Imagine you are the city election commissioner tasked with tallying one million paper ballots by morning. A single counting team working sequentially would take days. But you can exploit structure: divide the city into two districts of 500,000 ballots each, assign a team to each district, and have each district further divide into precincts of 250,000, then 125,000, until each precinct has a small pile that one person can count in minutes. When the counting is done, results flow back upward: a precinct supervisor adds two precinct totals to get a ward total; ward totals combine into district totals; district totals add to produce the city total.

The combination step at every level is trivial — just addition. The hard work (counting individual ballots) happens only at the leaves, and the recursive structure means there are only log₂(1,000,000) ≈ 20 levels. This is merge sort applied to vote tallies: the splitting creates a binary tree of subproblems, and the answers propagate back up to the root.

The crucial observation: a seemingly intractable problem on n items becomes two entirely manageable problems on n/2 items — and those become four problems on n/4 items — until the base case is trivially solvable. The key question is always: **how expensive is the combine step?** If combining two subsolutions costs O(n) and there are O(log n) levels, total work is O(n log n). This is the algorithm designer's fundamental budget.

sections.title: Recurrence Relations: Capturing Complexity Formally
sections.content:
Before writing a single line of code, a skilled algorithm designer writes the **recurrence relation** — a mathematical equation that describes how the running time T(n) of the algorithm on an input of size n relates to the running time on smaller inputs.

The general form for divide-and-conquer is: **T(n) = a · T(n/b) + f(n)**, where:
- **a** is the number of recursive subproblems
- **b** is the factor by which the input shrinks (b > 1)
- **f(n)** is the cost of the divide and combine steps (everything except the recursive calls)

Let us trace three algorithms:

**Merge sort**: divide into 2 subproblems of size n/2 (a=2, b=2). The merge step costs O(n) (d=1). Recurrence: T(n) = 2T(n/2) + O(n).

**Binary search**: divide into 1 subproblem of size n/2 — we pick one half and discard the other (a=1, b=2). Comparing the middle element costs O(1) (d=0). Recurrence: T(n) = T(n/2) + O(1).

**Quickselect** (average case): partition costs O(n), then recurse on one partition of expected size n/2 (a=1, b=2, d=1). Recurrence: T(n) = T(n/2) + O(n).

The recurrence fully encodes the algorithm's structure. Solving it gives the complexity. And the key tool for solving these recurrences is the master theorem.

sections.title: The Master Theorem: A Complexity Shortcut
sections.content:
The **master theorem** is a closed-form solution for recurrences of the form T(n) = a · T(n/b) + O(n^d), where a ≥ 1, b > 1, and d ≥ 0. It compares the logarithm log_b(a) — which captures how fast the number of subproblems grows — with d, which captures how expensive the combine step is. Three cases emerge:

**Case 1 (bottom-heavy)**: if log_b(a) > d, the recursion tree has more work in the leaves than at the top. The total cost is dominated by the leaf level: **T(n) = O(n^(log_b a))**.

**Case 2 (balanced)**: if log_b(a) = d, every level does the same total amount of work. With O(log n) levels each doing O(n^d) work: **T(n) = O(n^d · log n)**.

**Case 3 (top-heavy)**: if log_b(a) < d, the combine step at the root dominates all lower levels. Total cost: **T(n) = O(n^d)**.

Applying to our examples:
- **Merge sort**: a=2, b=2, d=1. log_2(2) = 1 = d. Case 2. **T(n) = O(n log n)**.
- **Binary search**: a=1, b=2, d=0. log_2(1) = 0 = d. Case 2. **T(n) = O(log n)**.
- **Quickselect (avg)**: a=1, b=2, d=1. log_2(1) = 0 < 1 = d. Case 3. **T(n) = O(n)**.
- **Strassen matrix mult**: a=7, b=2, d=2. log_2(7) ≈ 2.807 > 2 = d. Case 1. **T(n) = O(n^2.807)**.

The master theorem is not universally applicable — recurrences where subproblems have different sizes, or where f(n) has a logarithmic factor, may need other techniques like the Akra-Bazzi method. But for the overwhelming majority of divide-and-conquer algorithms you will encounter, it delivers an instant complexity answer.

sections.title: Merge Sort: The Canonical Divide-and-Conquer Algorithm
sections.content:
**Merge sort** is the textbook divide-and-conquer algorithm, and studying it deeply pays dividends across the entire paradigm. Its structure is clean: divide the array at the midpoint, recursively sort the left half, recursively sort the right half, then merge the two sorted halves into one sorted array.

The **merge step** is the heart of the algorithm and the key to its efficiency. Given two already-sorted arrays, you can merge them in O(n) using a two-pointer technique: maintain one pointer at the start of each array, always pick the smaller of the two current elements and advance that pointer. When one array is exhausted, append the remainder of the other. This runs in exactly n comparisons — no wasted work.

Why is merge sort O(n log n) and not O(n²)? The recursion tree has exactly ⌈log₂ n⌉ levels. At each level, the total amount of data being merged across all merge operations at that level is exactly n — just partitioned differently. So each level costs O(n) total. Multiplied by O(log n) levels: O(n log n).

Merge sort has two important properties not shared by all O(n log n) sorts:

**Stability**: equal elements preserve their original relative order. This matters when sorting objects by a secondary key after a primary key — a stable sort ensures you can chain sorts without disrupting earlier orderings.

**Predictable worst case**: unlike quicksort, merge sort is O(n log n) in all cases. There is no adversarial input that degrades it. This predictability is valuable in safety-critical systems.

The main drawback is **O(n) auxiliary space** for the merge — the merge step cannot easily be done in-place without becoming O(n log n) in space or O(n² ) in time. In-place merge sort variants exist but are complex and slower in practice. For most applications, the O(n) space cost is acceptable.

sections.caption: Merge sort recursion tree for [5,2,8,1,9,3]: divide to single elements (base cases), then merge bottom-up. Each merge level does O(n) total work; there are O(log n) levels.

sections.label: Example
sections.explanation: The `<=` in the merge comparison is what makes merge sort stable — when elements are equal, the left array's element goes first, preserving original relative order. The two-pointer merge visits each element exactly once: O(n) per merge, O(log n) levels of merging, O(n log n) total. The slice operations copy data, which is where the O(n) auxiliary space comes from.

sections.title: Quickselect: Finding the k-th Smallest in Expected O(n)
sections.content:
**Quickselect** solves the **order statistics** problem: given an unsorted array, find the k-th smallest element without fully sorting the array. A naive approach sorts in O(n log n) then indexes at k. Quickselect does it in **expected O(n)** — faster by a logarithmic factor.

The algorithm is a specialisation of quicksort's partition step. Choose a pivot, partition the array into three groups: elements less than the pivot (`less`), elements equal to the pivot (`equal`), and elements greater than the pivot (`greater`). After partitioning, the pivot elements occupy a contiguous block of sorted positions. If k falls within the less group, recurse on less with the same k. If k falls within the equal group, return the pivot. Otherwise, recurse on greater with an adjusted k.

**The critical difference from quicksort**: quicksort recurses on **both** partitions. Quickselect recurses on **exactly one** — the partition that contains position k. This cuts the total work roughly in half at each level.

Complexity analysis: with a random pivot, each partition splits the array into expected sizes around n/2 on each side. The recurrence for the expected case is T(n) = T(n/2) + O(n) — the O(n) partition cost plus recursion on half the elements. By the master theorem (a=1, b=2, d=1 → case 3, log_2(1)=0 < 1=d), T(n) = O(n). Each level costs n, then n/2, then n/4 — a geometric series summing to 2n = O(n).

**Worst case**: if every pivot chosen is the minimum or maximum, the partition produces one group of size n-1 and one empty. Quickselect then recurses on n-1 elements, giving T(n) = T(n-1) + O(n) → O(n²). Randomising the pivot makes this exponentially unlikely — the expected number of comparisons is below 4n regardless of input.

**The median-of-medians algorithm** provides a deterministic O(n) guarantee by choosing a pivot that always splits the array at least 30%/70%. It is more complex and slower in practice due to large constants, making randomised quickselect preferable outside of theoretical contexts.

The expected recursion depth is O(log n) but since work halves each level, the total geometric series sums to O(n). This is a beautiful example of how discarding half the problem at each step can change algorithmic complexity by a full logarithmic factor.

sections.title: Counting Inversions: Augmenting Merge Sort
sections.content:
One of the most elegant applications of divide and conquer is **counting inversions** in an array — a technique that demonstrates how a non-trivial problem can be solved by cleverly augmenting an existing algorithm.

An **inversion** is a pair of indices (i, j) where i < j but arr[i] > arr[j]. It measures how far an array is from being sorted: a fully sorted array has 0 inversions; a reverse-sorted array of size n has n(n-1)/2 inversions. Inversions arise in collaborative filtering (measuring ranking disagreement between two users), in genomics (measuring chromosome rearrangement), and in sorting complexity analysis.

The brute-force approach — check every pair — costs O(n²). But we can count inversions in O(n log n) by **augmenting merge sort**.

The insight: when we merge two sorted halves, any element from the right half that gets placed before elements remaining in the left half is in an inverted relationship with ALL remaining left elements. If right[j] is taken (because it is smaller than left[i]), then right[j] is also smaller than left[i], left[i+1], ..., left[left.length-1]. That is `left.length - i` inversions counted simultaneously in O(1).

By counting these **split inversions** during every merge, and accumulating them from both recursive subcalls, we count all inversions in O(n log n). This is a general technique: many counting and optimisation problems that seem to require O(n²) can be solved in O(n log n) by embedding the counting into the merge step of merge sort.

sections.label: Example
sections.explanation: The critical insight is in the else branch of mergeAndCount: when right[j] is less than left[i], we do not just count one inversion — we count all (left.length - i) inversions simultaneously, because left is already sorted and all remaining left elements are at least as large as left[i]. This batch counting within the O(n) merge step is what delivers O(n log n) overall, versus the O(n²) cost of checking every pair individually.

sections.title: Strassen's Algorithm: Reducing the Branching Factor
sections.content:
Matrix multiplication is a powerful demonstration of how divide and conquer can improve upon an already-reasonable algorithm by reducing the number of subproblems.

Multiplying two n×n matrices naively costs O(n³) — for each of the n² output entries, you compute a dot product of length n. The trivial divide-and-conquer approach splits each matrix into four n/2 × n/2 blocks and performs 8 recursive multiplications. Recurrence: T(n) = 8T(n/2) + O(n²). Master theorem: a=8, b=2, d=2. log_2(8)=3 > 2=d — case 1 — T(n) = O(n³). We recover the exact same O(n³) — no improvement.

**Volker Strassen's 1969 breakthrough**: reduce the 8 multiplications to 7 using algebraic trickery, at the cost of more additions. Additions cost O(n²) and additions do not affect the master theorem analysis when multiplications dominate. With a=7, b=2, d=2: log_2(7) ≈ 2.807 > 2 = d — case 1 — T(n) = O(n^2.807).

The improvement from 8 to 7 recursive calls is small by eye but enormous in its mathematical consequence: it moves the exponent from exactly 3 to approximately 2.807, shaving nearly a fifth off the exponent. For 1000×1000 matrices, Strassen is roughly 5× faster than naive. For 10,000×10,000 matrices, it is roughly 15× faster.

This illustrates a general principle: **in divide and conquer, reducing the number of subproblems (a) is often more impactful than improving the combine step (d)**, because a appears inside a logarithm in the exponent. Subsequent work by Coppersmith, Winograd, and others has pushed the matrix multiplication exponent below 2.376 using more elaborate algebraic constructions, though these algorithms have enormous constant factors that make them impractical.

Strassen also demonstrates a broader pattern: many divide-and-conquer improvements in algorithm design are algebraic — they find clever ways to compute the same results using fewer operations by reusing intermediate computations.

sections.title: Binary Search: Divide and Conquer Without Combine
sections.content:
**Binary search** is the simplest member of the divide-and-conquer family, and its simplicity reveals an important special case: sometimes the combine step costs nothing at all.

Given a sorted array and a target value, binary search compares the target to the middle element. If equal, found. If the target is smaller, it must lie in the left half — discard the right half entirely and recurse. If larger, recurse on the right half. This is pure divide-and-conquer with a trivial combine: there is nothing to combine because we recurse on only one subproblem and return its answer directly.

Recurrence: T(n) = T(n/2) + O(1). Master theorem: a=1, b=2, d=0. log_2(1)=0=d — balanced case — T(n) = O(log n). This is why binary search on a million elements takes at most 20 comparisons: ⌈log_2(1,000,000)⌉ = 20.

Binary search extends far beyond sorted arrays. The general pattern is applicable whenever you can identify a **monotone predicate** — a condition that is false for a contiguous prefix and true for the rest (or vice versa). You binary search on the predicate to find the transition point. This pattern appears in:
- Finding the leftmost position where a condition holds (lower bound)
- Finding the answer to an optimisation problem where feasibility is monotone in the answer (binary search on the answer)
- Finding a peak element in a unimodal array
- Square root, nth root computation to arbitrary precision

The requirement is not that you have a sorted array — it is that you have a **decision problem with a monotone answer**. When that structure exists, O(log n) binary search beats O(n) linear scan.

sections.title: Edge Cases, Common Mistakes, and Real-World Considerations
sections.content:
**Integer overflow in midpoint calculation**: The most famous bug in binary search implementations is computing `mid = (left + right) / 2`. When left and right are large integers near the maximum int value, their sum overflows. The safe version is `mid = left + Math.floor((right - left) / 2)`. This bug famously existed in Java's standard library `Arrays.binarySearch` for years.

**Off-by-one errors in binary search**: Whether to use `<` or `<=` in the loop condition, whether to set `right = mid` or `right = mid - 1`, depends on whether the search space is half-open or closed. Being sloppy about this causes subtle bugs that pass most test cases but fail on edge inputs. The solution is to be mathematically precise: define exactly what `left` and `right` represent (the search space is always `[left, right)`), and ensure the loop invariant is maintained at every step.

**Stack overflow in deep recursion**: Divide and conquer algorithms recurse to depth O(log n), which is typically fine (log₂(10^9) ≈ 30). However, quicksort with bad pivots recurses to depth O(n), which can overflow the call stack for large inputs. Iterative implementations or tail-call optimisation avoids this.

**Parallelism**: Divide and conquer is naturally parallel — the two recursive subproblems in merge sort are completely independent and can run concurrently on different CPU cores. Parallel merge sort achieves near-linear speedup with p processors up to p = O(n / log n). This makes divide and conquer a natural fit for multi-core and distributed systems (MapReduce is fundamentally a parallel divide-and-conquer framework).

**Cache performance**: Divide and conquer algorithms often exhibit excellent cache behaviour because they process contiguous subarray chunks that fit into cache. Algorithms like merge sort and quicksort often outperform their O(n log n) theoretical peers in practice because of cache locality, even if theoretical complexity is identical.

**When divide and conquer does NOT help**: If subproblems are not independent — if solving one subproblem requires the solution to another — you have overlapping subproblems and divide and conquer will recompute them exponentially many times. The fix is dynamic programming (memoisation). The canonical example is naive recursive Fibonacci, which is O(2^n) because it recomputes the same subproblems repeatedly.

**Historical context**: The term 'divide and conquer' in algorithm design traces to John von Neumann, who invented merge sort in 1945 as one of the first algorithms ever implemented on a stored-program computer. Binary search was described even earlier — D.H. Lehmer described it in 1946 — though a correct iterative implementation for all input sizes was not published until 1960. Strassen's matrix multiplication breakthrough in 1969 came as a surprise to the field, which had assumed O(n³) was optimal. It triggered an active research programme seeking the true matrix multiplication exponent that continues today. Quickselect was invented by Tony Hoare (also the inventor of quicksort) in 1961.

**Write the recurrence before you write the code.** The most important habit for designing divide-and-conquer algorithms is to state T(n) = a·T(n/b) + O(n^d) explicitly before implementing. If the master theorem tells you the combine step is the bottleneck (case 3), focus your optimisation there. If the recursion tree is bottom-heavy (case 1), reducing the number of subproblems (a) — as Strassen did — will improve the exponent. Also: **divide and conquer vs dynamic programming** is a common interview topic. The key question is whether subproblems overlap. If two branches of the recursion tree might solve the same subproblem, you need DP. If every subproblem is solved exactly once, pure divide and conquer is correct and efficient.

items: Divide and conquer has three mandatory phases: **Divide** (split into independent subproblems of the same type), **Conquer** (solve each recursively — base cases stop the recursion), and **Combine** (assemble subproblem solutions). Correctness follows by induction on the recursive structure.

The **master theorem** solves T(n) = a·T(n/b) + O(n^d) in three cases: if log_b(a) > d, the tree is bottom-heavy and T(n) = O(n^(log_b a)); if log_b(a) = d, it is balanced and T(n) = O(n^d log n); if log_b(a) < d, it is top-heavy and T(n) = O(n^d). Merge sort is balanced (O(n log n)); binary search is balanced (O(log n)); quickselect is top-heavy (O(n)).

**Merge sort** achieves O(n log n) because the O(n) two-pointer merge runs at O(log n) levels. It is **stable** and has predictable O(n log n) worst-case, but requires O(n) auxiliary space. The `<=` in the merge comparison enforces stability.

**Quickselect** finds the k-th smallest element in expected O(n) by partitioning around a random pivot and recursing on **exactly one** partition — not both. The geometric series n + n/2 + n/4 + ... = 2n confirms O(n). Worst-case is O(n²) with adversarial pivot choices, avoided by randomisation.

**Counting inversions** demonstrates augmenting merge sort: during the merge, when a right-half element beats remaining left-half elements, count `left.length - i` inversions at once. This reduces an O(n²) counting problem to O(n log n) by embedding the counting into the merge step.

**Strassen's matrix multiplication** shows that reducing subproblem count from 8 to 7 changes the exponent from 3 to log₂(7) ≈ 2.807 — a small change algebraically but a large practical speedup for large matrices. Reducing a (subproblem count) is often more impactful than reducing d (combine cost), because a appears inside a logarithm in the exponent.

Divide and conquer **requires independent subproblems**. If the same subproblem is solved by multiple branches of the recursion tree, dynamic programming (memoisation) is needed instead. The absence of overlapping subproblems is what distinguishes divide and conquer from DP.

quiz.question: What are the three mandatory phases of any divide-and-conquer algorithm?
options: Initialise, iterate, terminate
Divide, conquer, combine
Search, partition, memoize
Recurse, base case, return
quiz.explanation: Every divide-and-conquer algorithm has three phases: Divide (split the problem into smaller subproblems of the same type), Conquer (solve each subproblem recursively, with base cases solved directly), and Combine (assemble the subproblem solutions into a solution for the original problem). Correctness follows by induction on the recursive structure.

quiz.question: Merge sort's recurrence is T(n) = 2T(n/2) + O(n). Applying the master theorem (a=2, b=2, d=1), which case applies and what is the result?
options: Bottom-heavy: log_2(2) > 1, giving O(n^2)
Balanced: log_2(2) = 1 = d, giving O(n log n)
Top-heavy: log_2(2) < 1, giving O(n)
The master theorem does not apply when a equals b
quiz.explanation: With a=2, b=2, d=1: log_2(2) = 1 = d, which is the balanced case. The master theorem gives T(n) = O(n^d · log n) = O(n · log n) = O(n log n). Each of the O(log n) levels performs O(n) total merge work, giving the balanced case result.

quiz.question: How does quickselect differ from quicksort in its recursive structure?
options: Quickselect uses a min-heap to find the k-th element; quicksort uses in-place partitioning
Quickselect recurses on ONLY the partition containing position k; quicksort recurses on BOTH partitions
Quickselect is always O(n log n); quicksort is O(n) in the average case
Quickselect requires sorted input; quicksort works on any array
quiz.explanation: After partitioning around a pivot, quicksort recurses on both the less-than and greater-than partitions to fully sort the array. Quickselect only needs to find the k-th element: after partitioning, it recurses on exactly the one partition that contains position k, discarding the other. This changes the recurrence from T(n) = 2T(n/2) + O(n) = O(n log n) to T(n) = T(n/2) + O(n) = O(n) expected.

quiz.question: What is the worst-case complexity of quickselect, and what input causes it?
options: O(n log n) — when the array is already sorted
O(n²) — when the pivot is always the minimum or maximum element
O(n log² n) — when the recursion depth exceeds log n
O(n) always — a random pivot guarantees linear time regardless of input
quiz.explanation: If every pivot chosen is the minimum (or maximum) element, the partition produces one empty group and one group of size n-1. Quickselect then recurses on n-1 elements, then n-2, then n-3 — giving T(n) = T(n-1) + O(n) = O(n²). Randomised pivot selection makes this adversarial case extremely unlikely in practice, achieving expected O(n) on any input.

quiz.question: In the count-inversions algorithm that augments merge sort, when is a batch of inversions counted during the merge step?
options: When two equal elements are compared and placed in order
When a right-half element is placed before remaining left-half elements — each remaining left element forms an inversion with it
After the merge completes, by scanning the merged output array for pairs
When the array is initially divided into its two halves at the top level only
quiz.explanation: During the merge, if right[j] is less than left[i], then because left is sorted, right[j] is also less than left[i+1], left[i+2], ..., left[left.length-1]. Each of those constitutes an inversion (the left element has a lower index but higher value). Adding (left.length - i) to the count at this moment counts all these inversions in O(1), which is what makes the overall algorithm O(n log n) rather than O(n²).

quiz.question: Strassen's matrix multiplication uses recurrence T(n) = 7T(n/2) + O(n²). What is its complexity?
options: O(n²)
O(n² log n)
O(n³)
quiz.explanation: a=7, b=2, d=2. log_2(7) ≈ 2.807 > 2 = d — the bottom-heavy case. Master theorem gives T(n) = O(n^(log_2 7)) = O(n^2.807). Naive matrix multiplication has a=8, giving log_2(8)=3, so T(n) = O(n³). Strassen reduces a from 8 to 7 by using 7 multiplications and 18 additions rather than 8 multiplications, moving the exponent from 3 to approximately 2.807.

quiz.question: What property does merge sort have that quicksort typically does NOT, and why does it matter?
options: Merge sort is in-place; quicksort requires O(n) auxiliary space
Merge sort is stable — equal elements preserve their original relative order; quicksort is not
Merge sort runs in O(n log n) worst case; quicksort runs in O(n) average case
Merge sort uses iterative loops; quicksort requires recursive calls
quiz.explanation: Merge sort is stable: the `<=` comparison in the merge step ensures that when two elements are equal, the one from the left subarray is placed first, preserving original relative order. Quicksort's partition step typically swaps elements non-adjacently, destroying relative order. Stability matters when you sort objects by a secondary key after already sorting by a primary key — a stable sort preserves the earlier ordering.

quiz.question: Binary search has recurrence T(n) = T(n/2) + O(1). Which master theorem case applies?
options: Bottom-heavy (log_b a > d) giving O(n)
Balanced (log_b a = d) giving O(log n)
Top-heavy (log_b a < d) giving O(1)
The master theorem does not apply because there is only one subproblem
quiz.explanation: With a=1, b=2, d=0: log_2(1) = 0 = d, the balanced case. Master theorem gives T(n) = O(n^0 · log n) = O(log n). At each level, one comparison is done (O(1)) and the input halves. With O(log n) levels, total cost is O(log n). This is why binary search on one million elements takes at most 20 comparisons.

quiz.question: What is the key difference between divide-and-conquer and dynamic programming?
options: Divide and conquer always runs faster than dynamic programming
In divide and conquer, subproblems are independent and non-overlapping; in DP, subproblems overlap and the same subproblem is needed by multiple branches
Dynamic programming uses recursion; divide and conquer uses iteration
Divide and conquer requires sorted input; dynamic programming does not
quiz.explanation: In divide and conquer (merge sort, binary search), each subproblem is solved exactly once — the two recursive calls operate on disjoint portions of the input. In dynamic programming (Fibonacci, knapsack), multiple branches of the recursion tree need the same subproblem solution. Without caching, DP degrades to exponential time. Memoisation eliminates this recomputation, which is why DP applies only when there IS overlap — with purely independent subproblems, DP's caching adds overhead for no benefit.

quiz.question: What is the space complexity of merge sort and why?
options: O(1) — it sorts in-place like insertion sort
O(log n) — only the recursion call stack is counted
O(n) — auxiliary arrays for merging, with only O(n) total live at once despite O(log n) levels
O(n log n) — each of the O(log n) levels allocates a fresh array of size n
quiz.explanation: Each merge allocates a temporary array to hold the merged result. Critically, sibling merge operations do not run simultaneously — one completes before the other begins. At any moment on the call stack, the live temporary arrays total O(n) across all active frames, not O(n log n). The call stack itself is O(log n). So total auxiliary space is O(n). This contrasts with O(n log n) auxiliary for an algorithm that kept all intermediate results simultaneously alive.
